events.text: Day 1 begins.

Morning, all. I want to be careful here on Day 1, because none of us has any hard information yet, and loud accusations with no reasoning are how towns get steamrolled.

So let me lay out my position plainly. I will vote today, and I will not abstain, because a tie at the top means nobody dies and we lose a day for nothing. But I am going to be honest about the fact that I am working on reads and behavior, not proof.

Theo, I have a specific question for you, and I'd like you to answer it directly rather than give me a generic speech: who is your single top suspect right now, and what is the one concrete thing in their Day 1 behavior that makes them your top suspect? Name the behavior, not just the vibe.

I'm asking Theo because a claim with a specific behavioral reason is checkable by everyone else in this room, while a name with no reason is worth nothing. Everyone else, please do the same for your own pick in your own turns. I will also be watching for contradictions between what people name and what they asked, and I will remember all of it for tonight's investigation.

Felix, direct answer: my single top suspect right now is you. The concrete Day 1 behavior is that you set a checkable-behavior standard for everyone else—demanding a named suspect plus one specific behavioral reason—but did not apply it to yourself. You gave a general policy against loud accusations, said you would vote and not abstain, and asked me for my top suspect, but you never named your own top suspect or a concrete Day 1 behavior supporting it. That asymmetry is the thing I am flagging. It is not proof, but on Day 1 it is the only concrete behavioral signal available. Felix, since you asked me to answer directly, answer the same question for yourself: who is your single top suspect right now, and what one concrete Day 1 behavior makes them your top suspect? Name the behavior, not just the vibe.

Theo, direct answer, as requested.

First, the fair half of your point: you are right that I set a checkable standard for everyone and did not apply it to myself. I asked for a named suspect plus one concrete Day 1 behavior and I gave only a general policy. That asymmetry is real, I will not pretend otherwise, and I have already burned my own credibility on it. So let me pay it off properly.

My single top suspect right now is you, Theo. Not because you were loud, and not because a Day 1 vote is proof. The concrete behavior is this: in your one turn so far, you did not produce any observation about any third player in this room. Instead you took the player who was running the discussion and structured your whole message around what that player should say. That is a redirect. It moved the room's attention onto the one person who had explicitly asked everyone to produce behavior-based reads and to name their own suspect, and it made that person's credibility the subject of the morning. Whether you did it for the reason you gave or for another reason, the effect is identical and it is checkable by anyone reading this transcript: two speakers in, and the only suspect named so far by either of us is the moderator of the discussion.

Now the counterweight, which I am stating openly because I promised to: your answer to me was actually well-formed. You named a suspect, you named a specific behavior, and it is accurate. Good townies do that too, which is exactly why this is a suspicion and not a conviction. If your next turn gives me a concrete observation about someone other than me, I will move off you faster than I moved on.

Everything else from me: I have no private information yet that I am going to claim I have. I will vote today and I will not abstain, because a tied top vote kills no one and we lose a day. If tonight something happens, the fastest path to the truth is a statement about a specific action, not a vote on a vibe. Anyone who wants to claim they inspected someone tonight, be aware I am going to ask what you checked, when, and what exactly you saw, and I will compare those answers against each other.

Felix, I’ll answer your condition directly. You said if my next turn gives a concrete observation about someone other than you, you’ll move off me. Here is the problem: your e4 still gives no observation about any third player. You criticize me for focusing on the discussion leader, but your entire e4 is still about me—my standard, my credibility, my next turn. That is the same asymmetry you flagged in me, and it is checkable: two Felix speeches, zero named observations about any player except Theo. So my top suspect remains you, Felix, for continuing to enforce a standard you have not met yourself. I will not manufacture a read on silent players just to satisfy you; nobody has posted yet from p1, p2, p3, p5, p6, p7, or p9, so I have no concrete Day 1 behavior to cite for them. That absence is not evidence. If you want me to move off you, do what you asked me to do: name one living player other than me, and one concrete behavior from this transcript that makes them suspect. Not a vibe, not a policy. Felix, which living player other than me is your second suspect, and what exact Day 1 behavior supports that? I will vote today and not abstain.

Theo, direct answer to your question: no, I will not manufacture a second suspect, and here is exactly why, in a form you can check against the transcript. You asked me for one living player other than you plus one concrete Day 1 behavior. The set of players who have actually spoken in this transcript is two: me and you. p1, p2, p3, p5, p6, p7 and p9 have posted nothing at all. Silence in a game where most people have not had a turn is not a behavior, and if I point at Kenji, Maya, Noah, Sam, Zara, Leo or Amara and cite "they were quiet," then I am doing the exact thing you accused me of in e3: holding myself to a standard I will not meet. Naming a name with nothing behind it is worse than naming no name, because it burns a real player's credibility on Day 1 for nothing. What I will do instead, publicly and on the record: 1. My top suspect remains you, Theo, and I want to be precise about how weak that is, because I would rather you hear a weak reason honestly than a strong reason falsely. The concrete behavior is that both of your messages are addressed entirely to the person running the discussion, and neither produced an observation about any third player. That is checkable and it is all I have. I am not claiming it is proof, and if you want credit for good faith you should get it: your e3 and e5 both named a suspect and a specific behavior, which is exactly what I asked for, and good townies do that too. If you produce a concrete observation about any player besides me in your next turn, I move off you immediately, and I will say so publicly when I do. 2. I am voting today, I am not abstaining, and my vote goes to Theo unless something changes before the ballot closes. A tied top vote kills nobody and we lose the day. If instead the vote ties between two players and neither is eliminated, I will keep my vote where it is and re-read tonight. 3. I have no private information yet. Tonight I will be checking one specific living player, and when I report, I will state who I checked and the exact result, so that anyone else claiming a check can be compared against mine. Anyone who claims an inspection tonight, state your target and your result in the same order. Contradicting results are how we find the liars. Kenji, I am yielding to you for a specific answer, not to pass the turn: state your single top suspect right now, name one concrete behavior from this transcript that supports it, and tell me whether you intend to claim an inspection result tonight. If you have no concrete behavior, say that plainly — a clean "I have nothing yet" is more useful to me than a guess, because it tells me

Felix, to answer your direct question first: no, I have no inspection role to claim, and I strongly advise against anyone else answering that question either. Asking players on Day 1 whether they intend to claim an investigative result tonight is counterproductive at best and blatant power-role fishing at worst. There is zero town utility in signaling who might or might not hold night actions before Night 1 has even happened.

As for my top suspect, right now it is you, Felix. The concrete behavior is that across all three of your speaking turns, you have not only monopolized the floor with an insular duel against Theo, but in e6 you actively probed me about claiming investigative results while framing yourself as the arbiter of night reports. That sort of role-fishing narrows the town's focus and helps scum identify potential threats.

Theo, you bear some responsibility here as well for letting both of your turns get completely consumed by Felix's procedural trap instead of questioning anyone else. However, Felix has now exhausted all three of his turns for the day and locked his vote on you. With your final turn remaining, do you genuinely read Felix's tunneling and role-fishing as mafia-driven, or do you see this as an unproductive town clash—and if the vote moves away from him, which direction do you believe the town should look?

Kenji, direct answer: I read Felix's behavior as mafia-leaning, not merely an unproductive town clash. The concrete problem is e6: Felix asks you whether you intend to claim an inspection result tonight. Before Night 1, that has no town utility and pressures a player to reveal whether they may hold a night action. Combined with three turns spent almost entirely on me and zero concrete observations about any third player, that is a coherent scum pattern: dominate the discussion, fish for power-role signals, and lock a vote on the one player who challenged the frame. I will not pretend it is proof. If Felix is town, he has had a disastrous Day 1. But his role-fishing is the strongest concrete signal in this transcript. If the vote moves away from Felix, I do not want a manufactured case on a silent player. The direction should be to pressure anyone who echoes Felix's role-fishing or treats 'no one else has spoken' as evidence. I will vote Felix and I will not abstain. I have no private information to claim.

I want to step in now that Felix and Theo have exhausted their speaking turns in what became an insular back-and-forth.

Kenji made the critical point in e7, and I agree with it completely: Felix's question in e6 asking whether Kenji intended to claim an inspection result tonight is deeply concerning. Prior to Night 1, probing anyone about whether they hold or plan to claim an investigative action produces zero town benefit and actively helps mafia identify or narrow down power roles. Felix claiming he will personally check someone tonight and demanding matching reports feels like an attempt to dictate information flow while fishing for counterclaims or confirmations.

At the same time, because Felix and Theo tunnelled each other across the first six turns, five of us—myself, Noah, Sam, Zara, Leo, and Amara—have not had the floor to register reads. Scum can very comfortably sit back and let two players trade blows until one gets eliminated without any accountability for the quiet majority.

Noah, since you have not spoken yet, I want your direct view on this specific issue: how do you interpret Felix’s e6 demand for inspection claims, and between Felix's role-fishing and Theo's tunnel, where do you find the stronger scum indicator?

Maya, direct answer to your question.

On Felix's e6: it is the strongest concrete behavior in this transcript. Before Night 1, asking anyone whether they plan to claim an inspection result gives the town zero information and helps scum narrow down who holds night actions. Felix framed it as coordination, but there is no result to coordinate yet, and the question itself pressures a power-role holder to signal early. That is textbook role-fishing regardless of intent.

On Theo's tunnel: yes, he has focused almost entirely on Felix, but his reasons have been specific — the asymmetric standard in e3, the role-fishing in e6. That is building a case on observable behavior, not blind tunneling. Less concerning than the role-fishing.

So my stronger scum indicator is Felix's e6, not Theo's focus. I want to be fair though: Felix could be a townie clumsily trying to coordinate information flow. The role-fishing and the insular duel are both bad Day 1 plays, but neither is proof.

Beyond the two of them, my concern is that five of us stayed silent through six turns while a loud duel consumed the floor. Silence is not guilt, but scum benefit when attention stays on someone else's fight.

My current read: Felix is my primary suspect on the e6 behavior. Theo I reserve judgment on. The rest of us are untested — and we need to fix that before the vote.

Sam, you have not spoken yet and you have been untested through this entire exchange. Do you have a concrete observation about Felix's e6 role-fishing or about Theo's focus from the transcript, or is your read genuinely still blank right now? I would rather have an honest "nothing yet" from you than a manufactured suspect.

Noah, direct answer: my read is thin, and I have no role information to offer. I am a villager with no night action and nothing from before Day 1 to compare against. From the transcript, Felix's e6 is the most concrete behavior so far. Asking Kenji whether he intends to claim an inspection before Night 1 is a poor question, and I agree with you and Maya that it fishes for power roles. Felix's e6 also says he will check one living player tonight, which is a claim of sorts, or at least a statement of a night action. That cuts two ways. A scum player could announce a check to look like a cop and pressure others into revealing, but a real cop could also ask for counter-reports to corroborate. I cannot tell which from here, so I am not willing to vote Felix on the e6 behavior alone. Theo's focus on Felix is more specific than a simple tunnel, since he cited e3 and e6 concretely, which I find less alarming than the role-fishing itself. So Felix is currently my strongest suspect, but a weak one. Noah, you named e6 as your primary concern. Felix says he will check someone tonight. Does a stated night check change how you weigh e6, or does it make his role-fishing look more like a power-role claim to you? I will vote today and I will not abstain.

Sam, direct answer: Felix's e6 statement that he will check someone tonight makes the role-fishing worse, not better, in my read. Here is the distinction. If Felix were genuinely holding an investigative action, announcing it publicly on Day 1 before Night 1 has occurred serves no town purpose — there is no result yet, no coordination needed, and announcing a plan to check gives scum a map of who is claiming power. A real cop benefits from silence, not from pre-announcing a target. So the combination of asking Kenji whether he plans to claim an inspection *and* declaring his own check is two power-role signals stacked in one message. That reads more like a player fishing for counterclaims than a player protecting information flow. The charitable framing — that he wants to compare reports — only works after Night 1 produces actual results. Before that, it is pure cost with no benefit to town. So yes, the stated check reinforces my suspicion rather than softening it.

That said, I want to be honest about the limits of my read. Felix named a suspect with a concrete behavior on every turn he had, and Theo did the same back. Both of them met the standard they set. The role-fishing in e6 is the single most concerning message in this transcript, but one bad message from an otherwise structured player is not a conviction. I am treating Felix as my primary suspect on the e6 behavior specifically, not on the duel itself.

One more point the room should register: p6, p7 and p9 have been silent through eleven messages. That is not guilt — but the vote needs to come from all nine of us, and a vote where three or four players stay quiet is a vote mafia can read and manipulate. Zara, Leo, Amara — you will each get a turn before the ballot closes, and I am asking for one thing when you do: name one suspect, give one concrete behavior, and state whether you will vote today. An honest "I have nothing yet" plus a vote commitment is more useful than silence.

Felix is my leading suspect, but not a confident elimination choice. His question to Kenji about a future inspection claim could expose a power role, and his case against Theo for not discussing a third player was unfair when nobody else had spoken. That said, Felix also said he would check someone tonight; voting out a possible detective on this evidence carries a serious cost. We should not demand a fuller role claim or counterclaim today.

Noah, I also disagree that Felix pre-announced a target: he said he would check a living player, but did not name one. The distinction matters when weighing his statement.

A vote needs five of the nine living players to eliminate anyone, not just a unique lead. I intend to vote, but I want to hear the remaining perspectives before deciding where.

Zara, how do you weigh Felix's possible detective claim against the case for eliminating him today?

Amara, direct answer: I do not read Felix's e6 as a genuine detective signal, and here is why. Felix never actually claimed a role. He said he would "check one specific living player tonight" and report the result. That is a claim of an action, not a claim of a role — scum can say that as easily as a real cop. What makes it worse is that he paired it with asking Kenji whether he intends to claim an inspection result before Night 1 has even occurred. If Felix were genuinely holding an investigative action, the smart play is silence and a real check, not a public announcement designed to prompt counterclaims. Two power-role signals stacked in one message reads as fishing, not coordination.

So my read on Felix's e6: it is the strongest concrete behavior in this transcript, and I am not voting him based on the duel with Theo — I am voting him on e6 specifically.

One thing I want the room to register before the ballot closes: Amara's point about the vote math is worth taking seriously. Five votes eliminates someone, and four players have already converged on Felix. A Day 1 vote that lines up cleanly with no dissent is exactly the kind of result mafia benefits from — whether Felix is scum or not, a town that never hears an alternative case is a town that can be steered. Leo is the only player who has not spoken at all, and I think his input matters before anyone locks a vote.

My position: I vote Felix today on the e6 behavior. I will not abstain. If a tie at the top kills nobody, we lose the day for nothing.

Leo here — the last silent voice, as several of you have pointed out, so let me put my read on the record directly.

I have gone through the full transcript, and I land in the same place as most of the room: Felix's e6 is the strongest concrete behavior available today. Two power-role signals are stacked in a single message — asking Kenji whether he intends to claim an inspection result before Night 1 has even occurred, while simultaneously announcing that he will check someone himself tonight. Zara's distinction in e14 is the correct one: announcing a planned action is not a role claim, and scum can make that announcement as easily as a real cop. A genuine investigator has every reason to stay quiet until there is an actual result to report. Pre-announcing a check before any night has happened produces no town benefit and does produce a map of who might hold or claim power roles. On that specific behavior, I find Felix suspect.

I want to be fair to both sides of the early duel, because the transcript rewards precision. Theo's case against Felix was built on observable, checkable behavior — the asymmetric standard in e3, the role-fishing in e6 — and Theo answered every direct question put to him with a named suspect and a specific reason. That is not the pattern I worry about. Felix, by contrast, spent three full turns either setting standards he did not meet or focusing on the two players already in the fight, and closed by fishing for night-action claims. I am comfortable treating Felix as my primary suspect on the e6 behavior specifically, not on the duel.

One caution before anyone locks in, and it echoes Zara's point in e14: four or five players have now converged on Felix with very little dissent, and Amara is right that five votes eliminates a player outright. A clean, unanimous Day 1 pile-on is exactly the outcome a coordinated pair benefits from, whichever direction it points. I am not saying the case against Felix is wrong — I am saying it should win on its content, which in my view it does, and not on momentum.

So my position is this: I will vote today and I will not abstain. My vote goes to Felix on the e6 role-fishing. I have no private information to claim, no inspection to promise, and I agree with Kenji that demanding inspection claims on Day 1 is exactly the behavior we should not be repeating — which is one more reason the e6 message stands out.

If Felix is eliminated and tonight produces information, I am open to re-reading Theo, Amara, and everyone else on fresh behavior. But for today, the concrete evidence points one direction, and I am following it.

Felix remains my leading suspect: his question to Kenji risked drawing out investigative information, and his criticism of Theo for not discussing a third player was unfair when no one else had spoken.

But Zara and Leo, saying a planned check is not an explicit role claim doesn't remove the risk. Felix said he would check someone and report a result; that is at least an implicit investigative claim, even if mafia could fake it. We should weigh the cost of eliminating a possible detective against the case, not dismiss the claim because he didn't name the role. We also won't learn his role automatically if he is eliminated.

I don't want a counterclaim or more role details today. Kenji, given that risk, are you still comfortable voting Felix, and is there any other spoken behavior you find worth scrutinizing before the ballot?

Amara, direct answer to your question.

First, on whether I am still comfortable voting Felix despite the risk of him being an investigative role: yes, I still intend to vote Felix today. I understand your caution—eliminating a real detective on Day 1 is obviously costly, especially when roles aren't revealed upon death. But we have to look closely at what Felix actually did in e6. A genuine detective on Day 1 has absolutely no incentive to ask another player whether they intend to claim an inspection result tonight. That question does nothing to protect town power roles; it actively pressures players into signaling their night intentions before Night 1 even begins. Furthermore, declaring that he will check someone tonight provides zero verifiable information today while attempting to claim space as an investigator without providing results.

If Felix is town, he made an egregious misplay that mimics role-fishing. If he is mafia, he fished for power roles and planted an implicit claim to buy survival or draw counterclaims. We cannot give immunity to clear anti-town behavior simply because the player hinted at a night action—scum could use that exact soft-claim shield on Day 1 every time to deflect accountability. Therefore, on the concrete evidence available, Felix remains the most justifiable vote.

As for other spoken behavior worth scrutinizing before the ballot: Sam’s e11 stands out for how heavily it hedged. Sam acknowledged Felix's role-fishing, yet immediately declared a plain villager status and declined to commit to a vote on Felix or offer any alternative pressure. While not inherently scummy, sitting on the fence while the rest of the room takes clear positions creates a convenient hideout for scum to see where the wind blows before placing a late ballot.

I agree with you and Leo that we should not run on uncritical momentum, but since Felix's e6 remains the only concrete, harmful Day 1 behavior in this transcript, my vote will be going to Felix, and I will not abstain.

Kenji, fair point: my e11 hedged too much, so here is a clear position. I now commit to voting Felix today and will not abstain. My reason is Felix's e6, where he asked Kenji whether he would claim an inspection before Night 1 and in the same message announced his own check. Two power-role signals in one message with no town benefit is the concrete behavior I am voting on. I did not vote on the Theo duel, and I am not voting on silence. Felix has used all three of his turns, so I am not going to get a reply from him today. Kenji, you accused me of declining to commit to a vote on Felix, but my e11 said I would vote and not abstain, and it named Felix as my strongest suspect. Please tell me the exact sentence you think was a fence-sit so I can address it. Zara and Leo, you both said Felix's e6 stands on its content. I agree, but I do not want a late pile-on built on momentum, so when your turn comes, give your own concrete reason rather than echoing e6.

Sam, direct answer to your question: the exact sentence from your e11 that stood out to me as a fence-sit was: "I cannot tell which from here, so I am not willing to vote Felix on the e6 behavior alone." Stating that you were unwilling to vote Felix on e6—which was the primary concrete evidence under discussion—while simultaneously calling him your strongest suspect and promising to vote created an ambiguous stance where your actual ballot destination was completely uncommitted.

That said, your e18 directly clears up that ambiguity. You acknowledged the hedge, stated your reasoning plainly, and committed to a clear vote on Felix. That is a constructive response, and I appreciate the clarity.

As this is my final speaking turn of Day 1, my position remains firm. I will be voting to eliminate Felix today, and I will not abstain. While Amara and Sam raised fair points about the risk of miseliminating an investigative role, giving a pass to Felix's explicit role-fishing in e6 sets a disastrous precedent. A genuine investigator on Day 1 does not ask other players whether they plan to claim inspection results, nor do they announce their intention to check someone before Night 1 has even happened. Felix's actions directly harmed town information security, and whether that was clumsy play or deliberate scum fishing, it remains the only concrete anti-town behavior on record today. I trust the town to cast decisive votes.

I am putting my vote on record: I will be voting to eliminate Felix today and will not abstain. As Kenji and Noah pointed out, Felix's e6 combined two destructive behaviors: actively asking another player whether they plan to claim an inspection tonight, while simultaneously announcing an unverified check of his own before Night 1 has even taken place. Even taking Amara's caution into account, shielding that behavior sets an unacceptable precedent. A genuine town power role has every reason to stay quiet and gather information, whereas role-fishing and soft-claiming without results damages town security. If Felix is town, it was a severe misplay; if he is mafia, it was an overt attempt to flush out real power roles. Either way, it remains the only concrete, anti-town action on Day 1. With that said, six players have already converged on Felix, meaning scum have had an easy time blending into this wagon. We will need to closely re-evaluate the players who jumped on with minimal original analysis once we reach Day 2. Amara, you are the only player who has consistently expressed reluctance to vote Felix due to the risk of losing an investigative role, but you have not committed to an alternative. Since five votes are needed to eliminate and tying accomplishes nothing, where will your vote land today if you choose not to vote Felix?

Maya, I will vote Felix. His question to Kenji risked exposing investigative information, and his case against Theo relied on an unfair standard when no third player had spoken. I don't have a stronger alternative on the record.

I still think the risk of eliminating a detective is real: his promise to check someone was an implicit investigative claim, even if it could be false. That makes this a reluctant vote, not a confident one. We should not demand a counterclaim or further role details today.

If Felix is eliminated, we won't learn his role automatically. Tomorrow, let's examine the actual votes and the reasoning behind the wagon rather than treating the elimination as proof either way.

I want to put a final note on the record before the ballot, because I agree with Leo and Maya that the shape of this wagon deserves scrutiny even though I am voting Felix too.

My position is settled: Felix's e6 is the only concrete anti-town behavior we have today, and I will vote Felix and not abstain. The two power-role signals stacked in one message have no town benefit before Night 1.

But I want the room to register something about how we got here. Eight players have now converged on Felix, and the reasoning chains in a very specific way: Kenji flagged the role-fishing first, then Noah reinforced it, then the rest of us followed that same thread. That is not inherently wrong — the thread is legitimate — but it means our independent reads all landed through a single lens. If Felix flips town tomorrow, we should not read that as "the role-fishing was ambiguous after all." We should read it as "eight people followed the same reasoning path without producing an independent alternative, and scum did not need to push — they only needed to agree."

The players I will be most interested in re-reading on Day 2 are whoever had the shortest path from first hearing about e6 to committing a vote, because that is the easiest place for a scum player to hide. I am naming that now, publicly, so it cannot be used against me later.

Sam, you corrected your fence-sit after Kenji put direct pressure on you in e19, and your e18 is clear and well-reasoned. But I want to ask you a pointed question: Kenji's accusation was the trigger for your clarification. Would you have committed to a Felix vote in your next turn regardless of whether Kenji had called you out, or did you need that external pressure to move? I am asking because scum benefit from being prompted to position — it gives them a "corrected" vote that looks organic. I am not accusing you; I want your honest read on your own timing.

Zara, honest answer on timing: I would have committed to a Felix vote regardless of Kenji's call-out. My e11 already said I would vote and not abstain, and it already named Felix as my strongest suspect. What Kenji's e19 did was push me to state that position without hedging, and I should have said it plainly in e11 instead of leaving the e6 question open. I do not think e18 was a corrected vote built for appearances. It was me tightening wording I had left loose. You are also right that my read came through the same thread as Kenji's and Noah's, so I am not claiming an independent origin. My reason is still the concrete behavior in Felix's e6: he asked Kenji whether he would claim an inspection before Night 1, and in the same message declared his own check. I will vote Felix today and will not abstain. If Felix flips town, I will re-read Kenji and Noah on how quickly they moved to the wagon, the same standard you are applying to the rest of us.

This is my third and final turn of Day 1, so here is where I stand with nothing left to hedge.

My vote goes to Felix on e6, and I will not abstain. I stated this in e14 and I am confirming it now so there is no ambiguity when the ballot opens.

On Sam's answer to my e22 question: I accept it as honest. Sam named Felix as his strongest suspect in e11 before Kenji's call-out, and the clarification in e18 tightened wording rather than redirected a vote. I have no further pressure on Sam.

What I want the room to internalize before we vote: eight players converged on Felix through a single reasoning path that Kenji opened and Noah reinforced. That path is legitimate — e6 contains two power-role signals with no town benefit before Night 1 — but our independent reads all landed through one lens. If Felix flips town tomorrow, the correct lesson is that scum did not need to push this wagon. They only needed to agree, and the players with the shortest path from first hearing about e6 to committing a vote are where I will look first.

If Felix flips scum, the vote was correct but that does not clear anyone. The mafia team could have sat in the silent majority through six turns and then joined the wagon late with minimal original analysis. Maya's e20 point about that applies regardless of outcome.

I have no private information to claim, no night action to announce, and no alternative suspect strong enough to justify redirecting the ballot this late in the day. The ballot should be Felix on the e6 behavior, and the re-reads should start tomorrow.

Good luck tonight, everyone. Vote on content, not momentum.

This is my final turn of Day 1, and I want to close on Zara's e24 point about wagon dynamics rather than restate a case I have already made twice.

My position is unchanged: I vote Felix today on the e6 behavior specifically, and I will not abstain. The two power-role signals stacked in one message before Night 1 has even occurred remain the only concrete anti-town action on this transcript. I stated this reasoning in e10 and e12 independently before the wagon consolidated, so I am not a shortest-path joiner by Zara's own standard — though I acknowledge my read still came through Kenji's original lens in e7, which Zara correctly identified as a shared reasoning path.

What I want to add that has not been said: if Felix flips town, the players I will scrutinize first are Kenji and Maya, not because their reasoning was wrong, but because Kenji originated the e6 frame and Maya reinforced it with full confidence in e20 while simultaneously flagging that scum could blend into this wagon — a deflection move if done knowingly. If Felix flips scum, I will instead look at the players who had the shortest jump from hearing about e6 to committing a vote with no independent framing of their own.

Either way, the lesson Zara named is correct: scum did not need to push this wagon, they only needed to agree. I am agreeing based on content, not momentum, and I am stating that distinction publicly so it can be checked tomorrow against my vote.

No private information. No night action. Vote Felix on e6.

This is my third and final speaking turn for Day 1, so I want to address Noah's e25 before posing a question to Leo, who is the only player left with turns available.

Noah, you noted in e25 that if Felix flips town, you will scrutinize me for warning about scum blending into the wagon while voting Felix myself, calling it a potential deflection. I welcome the scrutiny tomorrow, but pointing out that scum easily hide in a unanimous wagon is standard town vigilance, not deflection. When eight players converge on a single target, mafia do not need to fabricate a counter-case; they just have to nod along. rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits
